questiontext.text:
An educational model for earthquake magnitude is

\( M=\log_{10}\left(\frac{A}{A_0}\right), \)

where \(A\) is the measured amplitude of seismic waves and \(A_0\) is a reference amplitude.

(a) An earthquake has a measured amplitude that is {@r1@} times the reference amplitude. Calculate its magnitude \(M\).

Enter your answer: [[input:ans1]]

[[validation:ans1]]

(b) A second earthquake has magnitude \(M={@m@}\). How many times greater is its measured amplitude than the reference amplitude?

Enter your answer: [[input:ans2]]

[[validation:ans2]]

(c) Two earthquakes have magnitudes \(M_1={@m1@}\) and \(M_2={@m2@}\).

How many times greater is the measured amplitude of the earthquake with magnitude \(M_2\) than that of the earthquake with magnitude \(M_1\)?

Enter your answer: [[input:ans3]]

[[validation:ans3]][[feedback:prt1]]

Give all answers as exact numbers.

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

Part (a): Calculating earthquake magnitude

The magnitude is calculated using the formula

\(M=\log_{10}\left(\frac{A}{A_0}\right)\).

The amplitude is {@r1@} times the reference amplitude, so

\(\frac{A}{A_0}={@r1@}=10^{@k@}\).

Substituting into the formula gives

\(M=\log_{10}(10^{@k@})\).

Using the logarithm rule \(\log_{10}(10^x)=x\), we obtain

\(M={@k@}\).

Part (b): Finding the amplitude ratio

The magnitude of the second earthquake is {@m@}. Using

\(M=\log_{10}\left(\frac{A}{A_0}\right)\),

we have

\({@m@}=\log_{10}\left(\frac{A}{A_0}\right)\).

Rewriting the logarithmic equation in exponential form gives

\(\frac{A}{A_0}=10^{@m@}\).

Therefore, the amplitude is {@r2@} times the reference amplitude.

Part (c): Comparing two earthquakes

The magnitudes are \(M_1={@m1@}\) and \(M_2={@m2@}\).

Using the magnitude formula for each earthquake,

\(M_1=\log_{10}\left(\frac{A_1}{A_0}\right)\), \(M_2=\log_{10}\left(\frac{A_2}{A_0}\right)\).

Subtracting the equations gives

\(M_2-M_1=\log_{10}\left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)\).

Converting to exponential form,

\(\frac{A_2}{A_1}=10^{M_2-M_1}\).

Substituting the randomized magnitudes gives

\(\frac{A_2}{A_1}=10^{@diff@}={@r3@}\).

Therefore, the measured amplitude of the second earthquake is {@r3@} times that of the first earthquake.
